lessons.title: Conventions
lessons.sub: Planes, axes, which segment moves, the pelvic convention
framing: Most confusion in this material is not about anatomy; it is about naming. The same pelvis can be called rotated left or right depending on whose textbook you open. This lesson fixes the vocabulary the rest of the course uses.

The course names the whole pelvis by the direction it faces in the transverse plane (oriented right or left), each hemipelvis by its own forward or backward rotation and anterior or posterior tilt, and every hip motion as either femur-on-pelvis (FA) or pelvis-on-femur (AF). These terms come from the Postural Restoration Institute and are credited on the About page.

Joint motion is named segment-on-segment: the first segment named is the one moving, and the second is the one held fixed. FA is the femur moving on a fixed pelvis (acetabulum); AF is the pelvis moving on a fixed femur. The same rule gives scapula-on-thorax (ST) and thorax-on-scapula (TS), and humerus-on-glenoid (HG) and glenoid-on-humerus (GH).

In standard anatomy, including Neumann, the innominate is the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis). This course borrows the word for any bony ring that positions a spinal region: the pelvic ring (lumbar), the rib cage ring (thoracic), and the cranium and mandible (cervical). This is course usage, not textbook usage.

lessons.title: Visceral anatomy
lessons.sub: Which side the lateralized organs sit on
framing: The thoracic and abdominal cavities are not mirror images. Unit 1 begins from the sides and levels of the major organs, so this lesson asks you to state them once.

It asks only where the organs are. What that asymmetry does, if anything, to posture and gait is a question for Unit 1. Side answers refer to where the greater part of the organ lies relative to the midline in the anatomical position.

lessons.title: Attachments
lessons.sub: Attachments of 23 muscles, in Neumann's terms
framing: For each muscle, choose its attachments from the list. The lesson uses Neumann's terms: proximal and distal for hip and shoulder muscles; inferior and superior for the diaphragm, erector spinae, rectus abdominis, and quadratus lumborum; lateral and medial for the obliques and transversus abdominis. Where a muscle has several attachments at one end, any one of them is accepted.
Fiber distinctions the course uses are listed as separate rows: diaphragm crural vs costal, adductor magnus anterior vs posterior head, and gluteus maximus upper vs lower fibers.

lessons.title: Distal-on-proximal actions
lessons.sub: Femur-on-pelvis, thorax-on-pelvis, scapula-on-thorax, and humerus-on-glenoid, with fiber distinctions
framing: Give each muscle's action in each plane, from anatomical position, with the first-named segment moving: the femur on a fixed pelvis for hip muscles (FA), the thorax on a fixed pelvis for trunk muscles (one side contracting), the scapula on the thorax for scapular muscles (ST), and the humerus on the glenoid for latissimus dorsi (HG).

Choose None where a muscle has no meaningful action in that plane. Some actions reverse with hip position (piriformis, adductor longus); answer for anatomical position. Lesson 6 asks the same muscles with the segments reversed: the proximal segment moving on a fixed distal one.
